note: The record of a routing change that actually happened, as distinct from the proposal that preceded it. The proposal stays marked PROPOSED_READY_TO_APPLY so the decision trail keeps both halves.

routes.json.domains['www.choicehotels.com']: mirrored, so a Choice property whose brand is unknown takes the same lane
routes.json.everything_else: byte-for-byte unchanged. Verified by loading the pre-change file from git and comparing every route row: the only two that differ are the two above.

providers.py.firecrawl: registered as an implemented provider, wrapping the existing measured adapter. The adapter itself was not rewritten.
providers.py.KNOWN_FUTURE_PROVIDERS: firecrawl removed. spider deliberately retained: it was benchmarked too, reached 7 of 25, and being measured is not the same as passing.
providers.py.capabilities: {runs_javascript, geo_pinnable} only. Not can_interact -- the routed lane runs a plain scrape; the deterministic interaction pass belongs to the benchmarks and is not claimed for production.
providers.py.profile: capture_kwargs pins firecrawl_capture.ROUTED_PROFILE, which is now the SINGLE definition shared with the benchmarks (firecrawl_hard_lanes_003.SCRAPE_PROFILE is the same object). Two copies could have let the routed lane drift away from the lane the decision was made about.

envelope.py + router.py.AcquisitionCost.reported_credits: plan credits, for lanes billed in them
envelope.py + router.py.AcquisitionCost.seconds_by_provider: wall-clock per lane, so a fallback's latency is visible instead of hidden in one total
envelope.py + router.py.AcquisitionCost.fallback_invoked: recorded as a fact rather than inferred from the length of providers_tried, which also grows when a provider is merely unhealthy
envelope.py + router.py.currencies: credits and usd_minor are separate fields and no total spans them. The Firecrawl plan endpoint reports an allowance, not a unit price, so there is no exchange rate anyone has measured.

normal_control.detail: routed to firecrawl, one attempt, VALID, publication-grade, identity confirmed, choice_static reader, fallback never invoked, 0 Browser API calls. Extraction reproduced the known refusal exactly.
normal_control.note_on_speed: 1.9s is faster than the profile's own 6s wait, so Firecrawl almost certainly served this from its cache. A credit was still consumed and a fresh 3.4 MB artifact was written, so the acquisition is real; the latency is not representative of a cold fetch.

forced_fallback.chosen_because: the Web Unlocker has a stable existing publication-grade benchmark for it, so a failure to reproduce would have been a real signal rather than an unknown
forced_fallback.sequence: firecrawl selected first -> 3 x ACCESS_DENIED (forced) -> router classified it TECHNICAL -> brightdata_web_unlocker selected second -> VALID -> choice_static reader -> identity confirmed -> publication-grade confirmed
forced_fallback.how_the_failure_was_forced: the registered Firecrawl provider's capture MODULE was replaced, inside the proof harness only, with one that returns ACCESS_DENIED carrying the vendor's own ALL_ENGINES_FAILED text and makes no request. It is restored in a finally block and the restoration is asserted. No credential, adapter, route or global was altered.
forced_fallback.significance: this path had never fired end to end. Every earlier work order could only record that it was untested.

falls_through: ACCESS_DENIED (this is what SCRAPE_ALL_ENGINES_FAILED maps to)
failure_semantics_preserved.rule: a second provider may retry a CHANNEL failure and must never re-interpret a SOURCE answer. Asserted through the real router with stub lanes, in both directions, rather than read back from the rule.
failure_semantics_preserved.PROVIDER_ERROR_note: the work order named PROVIDER_ERROR; the router's vocabulary spells the same thing CAPTURE_FAILED, NAVIGATION_FAILED and PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE, all of which escalate.
failure_semantics_preserved.POLICY_SURFACE_INCOMPLETE_note: The work order listed this among the failures that should fall through, and an earlier draft of this change moved it into ESCALATING. It was RESTORED to its pre-change classification before commit, on founder instruction, because it was the one change in the work order that was not Choice-specific: it splits the POLICY family and would alter every brand's ladder. It remains TERMINAL, exactly as it was. Nothing else in this work order depended on it -- no capture outcome maps to it, so the router cannot emit it, and neither live proof produced it.

reader_backlog_unchanged.item: no weight_limit is extracted from the wording 'A size limit of 40 pounds'
reader_backlog_unchanged.why_not: it is a coverage miss rather than a wrong fact, it is identical on both provider lanes, and a weight-pattern change re-reads every brand's corpus. It needs its own measurement.

freezes.credentials: FIRECRAWL_API_KEY and BRIGHTDATA_BROWSER_AUTH were supplied through the environment for the live proofs and appear in no file, report, log or commit.

known_behaviour_worth_naming.item: RoutingResult.failure is non-empty on a successfully-acquired fallback
known_behaviour_worth_naming.detail: the forced-fallback result carries state ACQUIRED_PUBLICATION_GRADE and failure ACCESS_DENIED at the same time. That is the router's existing design -- the failure is the only record of WHY the fallback ran -- but until this work order the path had never executed, so the combination had never appeared.
known_behaviour_worth_naming.consequence: state is the authoritative field. A consumer that reads success off an empty failure would now be wrong. Pinned by a test.

scope_note: Every change in this commit is confined to the Choice lane and to the provider registry that lane needs. No cross-brand routing semantics were altered.
